hook_text: A lemon, a nail and a coin can make electricity. Here is the chemistry inside every battery.
clip_script: Push a galvanised nail and a copper coin into a lemon, connect a meter, and it reads nearly one volt. You have built an electric cell. Every cell needs three things: two different metals and a juicy chemical between them. The zinc on the nail gives up electrons, the lemon juice lets charged particles move, and a current flows around the wire. Stored chemical energy becomes electrical energy, and a bulb or LED turns it into light. A torch cell works the same way, with zinc and carbon and a damp paste, giving 1,5 volts whether it is tiny or huge. Join cells nose to tail and their voltages add. That is a battery. Two cells give 3 volts. Six 2 volt cells give a car its 12 volts. When the chemicals run out, the cell is flat. Recharge it if you can, and recycle it when it dies.
visual_style: Close-up of a lemon cell with a meter reading; animated electrons moving out of zinc; a cutaway dry cell; cells clicking together into a battery with a voltage counter adding up.
pacing: Quick kitchen experiment, a calm look inside, then a stacking rhythm with numbers.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build a lemon battery to light an LED.
